title: The large majority of investor housing loans finance established dwellings rather than new construction
oneLiner: If the concession is meant to add rental supply, most of it is going to homes that already exist.
body: Lending data published monthly by the Bureau of Statistics shows investor loans for the construction or purchase of new dwellings are a small fraction of total investor lending. Most investor borrowing buys existing homes, where it competes directly with owner-occupiers.
contextBackground: This is the core factual plank of the new-builds-only proposal: it concedes that investment in new housing is valuable and argues the current concession is not producing it.
contextDisagreement: The figures are not contested. Defenders of the concession respond that buying an established home and renting it out still adds to the rental stock, even if not to the total stock.

evidenceItems.citation: Australian Bureau of Statistics, Lending Indicators — investor housing finance by purpose

otherClaim.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes

claimItself.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes
claimItself.oneLiner: The policy is now a bill before the Senate: negative gearing for new builds only from July 2027, existing investors grandfathered, and a reworked capital gains discount alongside it.
claimItself.body: The 12 May 2026 budget restricted negative gearing to newly built residential property for investments made after budget night, with effect from 1 July 2027, and replaced the 50 per cent capital gains discount with an inflation-based discount and a 30 per cent floor. Anyone using the concessions before budget night keeps them. A Senate inquiry took evidence in June 2026.
